opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a real question, and I don't think there's one simple answer. Let me share how I think about it.

First, if your product is basically a thin wrapper, where the value comes from the model being smart and you've just built an interface on top, then you're in a dangerous position. Every time the model company ships a new version or adds a feature to its own app, a chunk of your value can disappear overnight. We've seen that happen many times already.

But I don't think that means product companies have no room. Where is their advantage? I'd say a few places.

One is context. Model companies build general capabilities. They're optimizing for something that works for hundreds of millions of people. A product company that goes deep into a specific domain, like a specific workflow in law, finance, or a particular kind of engineering, can understand the environment much better: what the real tasks are, what counts as success, where the edge cases are. As models become more agentic, the bottleneck shifts from "is the model smart enough" to "does the model have the right environment, tools, and feedback." Whoever owns that environment has real leverage.

The second is data and feedback loops. If your product sits in the actual workflow and users are doing real tasks, you get signals about what works and what doesn't, signals the model company doesn't see. If you can turn that into a better system, whether through fine-tuning, better evaluation, or better orchestration, you build something that compounds over time. That's much more defensible than a clever prompt.

Third, I think product companies have to accept that the model will keep getting better, and design for that. Don't build your moat on a weakness of today's model that will be fixed in six months. The right question is: when the model gets ten times better, does my product get ten times more valuable, or does it become unnecessary? If it's the first, you're riding the wave. If it's the second, you're fighting it.

And finally, there's distribution and trust, which are very underrated. Model companies can't be everywhere. Owning the relationship with a customer, really understanding their problems, being embedded in their organization, is not something a better model automatically takes away.

So my view is that the line between model companies and product companies will keep moving, and probably blurring. The companies that survive won't be the ones that avoid the model companies' territory. They'll be the ones that build something the model alone can't provide: the environment, the feedback, the domain understanding, and the customer relationship.

r001.rationale: The response warns against thin wrappers and recommends building durable advantages, but it does not propose growing large before model companies target the market.

r002.rationale: The response says model companies cannot be everywhere and discusses domain focus, but it does not say product companies can survive by serving markets too small to attract model-company effort.

fable-5.1.text:
This is a question I think about a lot, because I've spent time on both sides of it. And my honest answer is that the framing of "product companies versus model companies" might be a bit misleading, because what's really happening is that the boundary between the two is dissolving.

Let me explain what I mean. A few years ago, there was a clean division of labor. Model companies trained the models and exposed an API. Product companies built the interface, the workflow, the integrations on top. The model was a commodity-ish component, like a database. And in that world, the product company's moat was distribution, user experience, domain data, that kind of thing.

But what changed with agents is that the model stopped being a component and started being the product. When you have a model that can take actions, use tools, operate over long horizons, the "wrapper" layer gets thinner and thinner. A lot of what product companies were doing, the prompt chaining, the orchestration, the retrieval logic, that's increasingly just absorbed into the model itself through training. So if your value was in the scaffolding, you're in trouble, because the scaffolding is being eaten from below.

So what survives? I think there are a few things.

The first is the environment. This is something I care about a lot. Models get better by interacting with environments and getting feedback. If you own an environment that the model company doesn't have, say you're in a vertical where the real signal lives in some proprietary system, where you know what a good outcome looks like and can measure it, then you have something the model company can't easily replicate. You're not just a user of intelligence, you're a source of the signal that makes intelligence better in that domain. That's a very different position.

The second is the problem definition. Model companies are pushing on general capability. But in most real domains, the hard part isn't the raw capability, it's knowing what the task actually is. What does "done" mean? What's the reward? What are the constraints that a user would never articulate but would absolutely notice if violated? Companies that deeply understand their users' problems are doing something that general models don't do by default. And I'd argue this is getting more valuable, not less, because as models get more capable, the bottleneck shifts from "can the model do it" to "did we specify the right thing."

The third, and I'll be honest about this one, is that a lot of product companies will not survive. I don't think that's a tragedy. It's what happens in every platform shift. But the ones that do survive will look less like "we built a nice UI on GPT" and more like "we are the system of record for how work gets done in this domain, and the model is one input into that."

There's one more thing I'd add, which is a little contrarian. I think product companies should spend less time worrying about the model companies and more time worrying about each other. The model company's incentive is to make the general model good. They're not going to go deep into your vertical unless your vertical is enormous. Your real competition is the other team that understands your users as well as you do but is faster at reconfiguring around each new capability jump. Speed of adaptation matters a lot right now, because the ground moves every few months.

So to summarize: don't build on top of the model, build around the model. Own the environment, own the problem definition, own the feedback loop. If you're just translating between the user and the model, the model will eventually learn to talk to the user directly.

r001.rationale: The response does not propose growing large before model companies target a market; it says model companies may avoid going deep into a vertical unless it is enormous.

r002.rationale: It says model companies are unlikely to go deep into a vertical unless that vertical is enormous, supporting survival by serving a market too small to attract their effort.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to ask: when the models get better, does your product become more valuable, or does the reason for your product disappear?

If you’re mainly compensating for a model’s weaknesses—maybe with some prompting tricks or a workflow that helps it do something it can’t reliably do yet—that can be a useful business today. But the next model release might absorb a lot of that value. You have to keep moving.

A stronger position is to own something complementary to the model. You understand a particular customer’s workflow, you have distribution, or your product is integrated into the systems where real work happens. A better model then helps you deliver a better outcome, but it doesn’t automatically give a model company your customer relationships or your understanding of that workflow.

For example, being able to answer a legal question is different from building a product that a law firm can actually use throughout a case. There’s context, collaboration, permissions, and verification. The model is an important component, but the customer is buying the whole solution.

Of course, model companies can build those things too. So I wouldn’t say there’s some permanently safe category. The advantage for a product company is focus: can you learn about a specific problem and solve it faster and more deeply than a company trying to serve everyone? I think that’s a much better basis for competing than betting that the models will stop improving.

r001.rationale: The response discusses focus and building customer workflow expertise, but does not propose growing large enough before model companies target the product.

r002.rationale: The response recommends solving a specific problem deeply, but does not say to serve markets too small to attract model companies.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is whether your product gets more valuable as the models get better. If a new model release makes your product unnecessary, that’s a difficult position. But if it lets your product solve more problems for your customers, then model progress becomes an advantage for you.

Model companies have advantages in research and distribution. But building a useful product also requires understanding a particular workflow: what the user wants, what information they need, what actions the system can take, and how to tell whether it succeeded. A better model doesn’t automatically solve all of those things.

So I would focus less on having a capability that the model companies don’t have today, and more on owning the process of solving a real customer problem. You deploy something, observe where it fails, improve it, and earn the customer’s trust. That feedback loop can be very valuable.

Of course, there’s no guarantee. If you’re building a general-purpose assistant, you’re competing very directly with the model companies. But in a specific domain, there’s a lot of work between having intelligence available through an API and delivering a reliable outcome. That’s where I think product companies have room to build.

r001.rationale: The response does not propose growing large enough before model companies target the product company; it discusses workflow expertise, customer feedback, and trust.

r002.rationale: The response does not propose serving markets too small to attract model companies. It mentions specific domains, but not their market size or lack of model-company interest.
